parts.title: Listening Part 1 会話の穴埋め
parts.desc: 2人の日常の会話（申し込み・問い合わせ）を聞いて、メモの空所を10問埋める
parts.tip: 先にメモ全体を見て、空所に入るのが名前・数字・日付・名詞のどれかを予想する。答えの直前に「いったん言って訂正する」ひっかけが多いので、最後に確定した情報を書く。つづりを言う名前は1文字ずつ書き取る。

W: Good morning, Riverside Leisure Centre, Helen speaking. How can I help?
M: Oh, hello. I'm thinking of joining the centre, and I wanted to find out a bit more about membership before I come in.
W: Of course. I can tell you about the options and, if you like, I can take your details and set up the membership over the phone. It saves a lot of time when you arrive.
M: That would be great, thanks.
W: Lovely. Could I start with your name?
M: Yes, it's Daniel Pelham.
W: Could you spell your surname for me, please?
M: Sure. It's P-E-L-H-A-M.
W: Thank you, Mr Pelham. And your address?
M: It's 14 Garnet Road. That's G-A-R-N-E-T.
W: Garnet Road. Is that the one near the old railway station?
M: That's right, just behind it. I moved there in the autumn, so I'm still getting to know the area.
W: Well, you're only ten minutes away from us, then. Now, when would you like your membership to begin?
M: I was going to say the first of March, but actually I'm away that weekend, so could we make it the third instead?
W: The third of March. No problem at all. Now, we have three types of membership. There's Bronze, which covers the gym, but only at quieter times of the day, so not in the early morning or the evening.
M: That wouldn't work for me. I'm at work all day.
W: Then there's Gold, which includes absolutely everything: the swimming pool, the tennis courts, all the classes.
M: To be honest, I'm not much of a swimmer, so Gold sounds like more than I need. Is there something in between?
W: Yes, that's Silver.
M: Then I think Silver is probably the one for me. What does it include?
W: With Silver you can use the gym at any time we're open, and you also get the sauna.
M: But not the pool?
W: No, I'm afraid not. The pool is only included in Gold.
M: That's fine. And how much is Silver?
W: It used to be thirty-two pounds a month, but the prices went up in January, so it's now thirty-four pounds a month.
M: That's still cheaper than my old gym, so I'm happy with that. Do I have to sign up for a whole year?
W: No, there's no minimum contract. You just give us one month's notice if you want to leave.
M: Oh, that's good to know.
W: Good. Silver members can also join one class a week free of charge. Most people choose yoga, but the yoga classes are nearly always full, so I'd suggest Pilates, which usually has spaces.
M: I did Pilates years ago and quite enjoyed it. I'll go for that.
W: Great. Now, when you come in for the first time, we'll need to make your membership card. Could you bring a photograph with you?
M: A photograph. Do you need proof of address as well, like a bank statement?
W: No, we don't ask for that any more. We can check your address online. Just the photo.
M: Fine. Is there anything else I need to do before I start using the gym?
W: Yes, every new member has an induction with one of our trainers. They show you how to use the machines safely. The next sessions are on Tuesday evening and Thursday evening, both at seven.
M: I play football on Tuesdays, so Thursday would be better.
W: I'll put you down for Thursday, then. It takes about forty-five minutes, so wear something comfortable.
M: Will do. Oh, one more thing. I'll probably drive. Is there much parking?
W: Our own car park is quite small, and it's usually full in the evenings, so we ask members to use the car park behind the library. It's only a two-minute walk, and it's free after six o'clock.
M: Behind the library. That's easy. Well, thank you very much, Helen. You've been really helpful.
W: You're welcome, Mr Pelham. We'll see you on Thursday.

M: Good afternoon, Coastline Cycle Hire. Mark speaking.
W: Hello. I'd like to hire some bikes for a family holiday in August, and I wondered if you could help.
M: Certainly. Let me just open a booking form. Could I have your name, please?
W: Yes, it's Anna Whitlock.
M: Is that W-H-I-T-L-O-C-K?
W: That's right.
M: Thank you, Mrs Whitlock. And which dates are you looking at?
W: We arrive on the twelfth of August, so we'd like the bikes from that day. We were planning to keep them until the sixteenth, but my husband has just managed to get a few more days off work, so can we say until the eighteenth?
M: From the twelfth to the eighteenth of August. That's fine; we still have plenty of bikes for that week. How many will you need?
W: Two adult bikes for my husband and me, and a child's bike for our son, who's eight.
M: Two adult and one child's bike.
W: And my father is coming with us. He's in his seventies and he's quite fit, but the hills around there worry him a bit, so we thought he might like an electric bike.
M: That's a very popular choice. Most of our older customers go electric now. So that's one electric bike as well.
W: Lovely. And we have a daughter who's only two. What would you recommend for her?
M: Well, a lot of people ask about child seats, but we've found that a trailer is safer and more comfortable for very young children, and it can carry a bag as well. So I'd go for a trailer.
W: A trailer, then. Now, could you tell me the prices?
M: Of course. The adult bikes are fifteen pounds a day and the child's bike is eight pounds a day. The electric bike is normally twenty-five pounds a day, but because you're hiring it for more than five days, you get the weekly rate, which works out at twenty-two pounds a day.
W: Twenty-two. That's not bad. And does that price include insurance?
M: Yes, basic insurance is included in all our prices, so if a bike is stolen while it's locked, you won't have to pay for it.
W: Good. Is there a deposit?
M: Yes. We take a deposit of fifty pounds for each bike, which we return when the bikes come back undamaged. We take it by card, not cash.
W: That's fine. And are helmets included?
M: Yes, helmets are free, and so are locks. The only things that cost extra are baskets, which are two pounds a day each, if you want them.
W: I think one basket would be useful for picnics. Could you add one?
M: One basket. Done. Now, where would you like to collect the bikes? We normally have two shops, one by the station and one on Mill Street, but the station shop is closed for repairs until September.
W: So Mill Street, then.
M: Yes, Mill Street. It's just behind the harbour, and the bikes will be ready from nine in the morning.
W: Do I need to bring anything with me?
M: Just some identification. A driving licence is fine, but if you're coming from abroad, a passport is better.
W: We're coming from Germany, actually, so I'll bring my passport.
M: Perfect. Is there anything else I can help you with?
W: Well, can you suggest a good route for a family? Nothing too difficult.
M: Most families love the path along the old railway line. It's completely flat, there's no traffic, and it goes all the way to Westcombe, where there's a nice café and a beach.
W: That sounds ideal. How far is it?
M: About eleven kilometres each way, so it's a comfortable day out, even for your son.
W: Wonderful. Thank you so much.
M: My pleasure. I'll email you a confirmation this afternoon.

W: Hello, is that Oakfield Community Hall?
M: Yes, it is. This is Peter, the bookings manager. How can I help you?
W: Hi, Peter. I'm organising a retirement party for a colleague, and a friend said your hall might be suitable. Could I ask a few questions?
M: Of course. Let me take a few details first. What's your name?
W: Joanna Fenwick.
M: Could you spell the surname?
W: Yes, F-E-N-W-I-C-K.
M: Thank you, Ms Fenwick. And when are you planning to hold the party?
W: We were hoping for Saturday the fourteenth of June.
M: Let me check. Oh, I'm sorry, the fourteenth is already booked for a wedding. What about the following Saturday, the twenty-first?
W: The twenty-first should be fine. Most people are free then, I think.
M: Good. I'll put a provisional booking on the twenty-first. How many guests are you expecting?
W: At first we thought about fifty, but more people have said yes than we expected, so it'll be closer to sixty.
M: Sixty. Is there enough parking for that many people?
W: I was going to ask about that.
M: There are about thirty spaces at the front, and the street behind the hall is free in the evenings, so it shouldn't be a problem. Now, with sixty guests, I wouldn't recommend the Main Hall. It holds two hundred, and with only sixty people it can feel rather empty.
W: What else do you have?
M: We have the Garden Room, which is perfect for groups of forty to eighty. It has big windows and opens onto the lawn, so on a warm evening people can go outside.
W: The Garden Room sounds lovely. How much does it cost?
M: For an evening booking, from six o'clock, it's one hundred and eighty pounds.
W: And is there a deposit?
M: Yes, there's a deposit of seventy-five pounds, which we return after the event as long as the room is left in good condition.
W: That seems reasonable. What about food? Do we have to bring our own?
M: You can, but we also work with a local caterer who can provide either a cold buffet or a hot buffet. Most people choose cold in the summer, but you can decide.
W: My colleague loves a proper meal, so I think we'll go for the hot buffet.
M: I'll make a note of that. Do any of your guests have special requirements?
W: Yes, several of them are vegetarian, so we'll need some vegetarian options. Nobody has mentioned any allergies so far, but I'll ask again.
M: Fine. The caterer will contact you nearer the time. Now, will you want music?
W: Yes. We thought about a live band.
M: I'm afraid we can't allow live bands any more because of complaints from the neighbours. But the Garden Room has its own sound system, and you're welcome to plug in a phone or a laptop.
W: Oh, that's fine. We'll just make a playlist and use the sound system.
M: And I should mention that all events on a Saturday have to finish by eleven o'clock. On Fridays it's midnight, but on Saturdays it's eleven.
W: Eleven is fine. Most of the guests will be quite tired by then anyway. Can we come in earlier to decorate the room?
M: Yes, you can, but please don't stick anything on the walls with tape, because it damages the paint. There are hooks along the walls for banners and balloons.
W: Hooks. That's good. We'll bring some string.
M: One last thing. On the night, the person to contact if anything goes wrong is our caretaker, Mr Doyle.
W: How do you spell that?
M: D-O-Y-L-E. He'll be there from five to let you in and help you set up.
W: That's very helpful. Can I confirm the booking now?
M: Yes. I'll email you a form this afternoon, and once you've paid the deposit, the booking is confirmed.
W: Perfect. Thank you, Peter. You've been very helpful.
M: Not at all. I hope your colleague enjoys the party.

M: Good morning, Central Bus Station lost property office. How can I help?
W: Oh, hello. I think I left a bag on one of your buses yesterday, and I'm hoping someone has handed it in.
M: I'm sorry to hear that. Let me take some details and I'll check our records. First of all, what kind of bag was it?
W: It's a rucksack. Not a big one, just the kind you'd take on a day trip.
M: A rucksack. And what colour is it?
W: It's green. Most people think it's black when they see it, but it's actually a very dark green.
M: Dark green. Is there anything unusual about it, anything that would help us recognise it?
W: Yes, there's a small badge on the front pocket with a picture of a mountain on it. My brother gave it to me after a walking holiday.
M: A badge with a mountain. That's helpful. Can you tell me what was inside?
W: Well, luckily my laptop wasn't in it. I'd left that at home. But there was a camera, which is the thing I'm most worried about, and an umbrella, and a library book.
M: A camera, an umbrella and a library book. Do you know which bus you were on?
W: Yes. I usually take the number seventy-four into town, but yesterday I was going to see a friend, so I took the forty-seven.
M: The forty-seven. And that was yesterday, so Tuesday the ninth of October?
W: That's right, Tuesday the ninth.
M: And where did you get off?
W: At the stop outside the hospital. My friend works there, and we were meeting for lunch. I realised the bag was missing when I sat down in the café.
M: Right. Let me look on the computer. Hmm, I can see several bags that came in from the forty-seven yesterday, but none of them is described as a green rucksack. That doesn't mean it isn't here, though. Sometimes items take a day or two to reach us from the depot.
W: Oh, I see. Which depot is that?
M: It's the one on the edge of town, near the industrial estate. All the buses go back there at night, and the cleaners check them and send anything they find to us the next morning. But if the bag was found late in the day, it might still be at the depot.
W: Could I just go to the depot myself?
M: I'm afraid not. It isn't open to the public, so everything has to come through this office.
W: Oh, I see.
M: So what I'll do is make a report, and if it turns up, we'll contact you. Could I have your name, please?
W: Clara Corrigan.
M: Could you spell your surname?
W: C-O-R-R-I-G-A-N.
M: Thank you. And how would you like us to contact you? By phone or by email?
W: I'm in meetings most of the day, so email would be better. I check it all the time.
M: Email, then. I'll take your email address in a moment. Now, a couple of things you should know. If we find the bag, you'll need to collect it in person from this office, and you'll need to bring some photo identification.
W: That's fine. Is there a charge?
M: There's a small handling fee of three pounds, unless the item is a wallet or a bag containing a bank card, in which case it's free.
W: Three pounds is no problem. And what are your opening hours?
M: We're open from eight until six, Monday to Saturday. We're closed on Sundays.
W: Good, I can come in on my way to work. How long do you keep things?

M: We used to keep items for thirty days, but we've changed that recently, so now it's twenty-eight days. After that, anything that hasn't been collected is given to charity.
W: Twenty-eight days. Well, I hope I'll hear from you long before that.
M: I'm sure you will. Most items are found within a few days. Now, could I take that email address?
W: Of course. It's ...

sets.script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Greenfield Community Library. My name is Sarah, and I coordinate the volunteer programme here. Before we start the tour, let me explain how the programme works. The library is open six days a week, but volunteers are only needed from Tuesday to Saturday, because Monday is our quietest day and the paid staff can manage on their own. Most of you will do one shift a week, and a shift lasts three hours. You can choose a morning shift, which runs from nine to twelve, or an afternoon shift, from one to four. We no longer offer evening shifts, as the building closes at five. Now, what will you actually do? There are four main roles. The first is shelving: putting returned books back in the right place. It sounds simple, but it is the job that saves us the most time. The second is the welcome desk, where you greet visitors and help them find things. You do not need to know everything; you just need to know who to ask. The third role is the children's story hour, which happens every Wednesday and Saturday morning. If you enjoy reading aloud, this is for you. And the fourth is the computer corner, where you help older visitors with email and online forms. We also have a small cafe, but that is run by a separate company, so volunteers do not work there. A few practical points. Please wear your name badge whenever you are in the building. Lunch is not provided, but you are welcome to use the staff kitchen, which has a fridge and a kettle. If you cannot come to a shift, please send a text message to the number on your badge at least a day before. Finally, after you have completed ten shifts, you will receive a certificate, and after twenty, we will give you a free library card for a friend or family member. Right, if everyone is ready, let's begin the tour on the ground floor.

choices: Volunteers usually work once a week.
A shift is three hours long.

sets.script:
Thank you for inviting me onto the programme. As many of your listeners will know, the Elmfield Community Garden opens to the public next Saturday, and I'd like to explain what people can expect when they visit.

First, a little history. The site, on the corner of Bridge Street, was a car park for almost forty years. When the council decided that it was no longer needed, a group of local residents asked whether it could become a green space instead, and after a long campaign they got their wish. The ground, as you can imagine, was in a terrible state, so the first job was to bring in fresh soil, more than three hundred lorry loads of it. That took most of last winter. Since then, nearly all the work has been done by volunteers. The one exception is the paths, which were laid by a professional company, because they had to be suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs.

So what will you find in the garden? Just inside the main gate are the vegetable beds. These are divided into small plots, and local families can rent one for a year for a very small fee. We expected perhaps thirty applications, but in fact we received well over a hundred, so the plots will be given out in a draw next month, and we're already looking for land nearby for a second garden.

Beyond the vegetable beds there's an orchard with apple, pear and plum trees. They were only planted this spring, so please don't expect to pick any fruit this year. It will be at least three years before there's a proper harvest, and when there is, the fruit will be shared among the volunteers and the local primary school.

At the far end is the wildlife area, with a pond and an area of long grass. We've deliberately left this part a little wild, and we ask visitors to keep to the wooden path there. That's mainly to protect the frogs, which moved into the pond within weeks of it being dug. Dogs are welcome in the garden, by the way, as long as they're on a lead.

Now, the opening day itself. The gates open at ten. A lot of people have asked me whether a celebrity will be cutting the ribbon. We did discuss inviting someone from television, but in the end we decided that the honour should go to Mrs Joan Ellis, who started the campaign twelve years ago and who is now ninety-one.

During the day there'll be guided tours of the garden every hour, and there'll be a plant sale, with all the money going towards new tools and seeds. We had also planned a cooking demonstration using vegetables from the garden, but unfortunately the chef is no longer able to come, so that won't be happening. And for those of you who asked about the seed swap, that will now take place in the autumn, when there are more seeds to share.

A practical point: there's no parking at the garden, which I know is rather ironic, given its history. So we strongly recommend coming by bus. The number twelve stops right outside the gate.

Finally, people often ask how they can help. We're not asking for money. The council has given us a grant that covers our costs for the first two years. And we have more garden tools than we can store, thanks to some very generous neighbours. What we really need is people. Our volunteer sessions are every Sunday morning from nine until twelve, and you don't need any experience. Just turn up in old clothes, and we'll find you something to do.

sets.script:
Good afternoon, and welcome to Ashby Mill. My name's Richard, and I'll be your guide for the next hour. Before we go inside, let me tell you a little about the building.

There has been a mill on this part of the river for a very long time. The first one is mentioned in records from the thirteen hundreds, but nothing of that early building survives. The mill you can see in front of you was built in the late seventeen hundreds, in 1792 to be exact, and it ground flour for the surrounding villages for over a century and a half.

People often assume that the mill closed because of the fire in 1921. There was certainly a fire, and you can still see the black marks on some of the beams upstairs. But the damage was repaired, and the mill carried on working. What finally closed it, in 1956, was competition from large modern factories, which could produce flour far more cheaply. After that the building was used as a store for a while, and then it stood empty for nearly forty years.

The restoration was carried out by a charitable trust, and it took eleven years. The hardest part was the water wheel, which had to be completely rebuilt using the original drawings. The mill reopened in 2015, and I'm pleased to say that it now grinds flour again, using exactly the same method as in the eighteenth century.

Now, a few rules before we start. The mill is a working building, so when the machinery is turning, please keep your hands well away from it. Some of the moving parts are not behind barriers, because we want you to see how they work. Also, the stairs are very narrow and steep, so I must ask you to leave any large bags or rucksacks at the reception desk. You're very welcome to take photographs anywhere in the building, including with a flash, and you can bring drinks in with you, as long as they have a lid.

Let me explain the layout. We'll begin on the ground floor, where the water wheel drives the machinery. From the viewing platform there, you can watch the wheel turning through a glass panel in the floor. Most visitors say it's the highlight of the visit.

On the first floor are the millstones themselves. There are two pairs, and on Wednesdays and Saturdays you can watch the miller at work, grinding the grain. On other days the stones are still, but there are guides who will explain the process.

The top floor was where the grain was stored in sacks. Today it houses a small exhibition about the lives of the people who worked here, with photographs, letters and some of the miller's tools. There's also a short film about the restoration, which lasts about ten minutes. I'd recommend sitting down to watch it at the end of the tour.

Outside, in the old stable yard, you'll find the café. All the cakes are made with flour from the mill, and I can personally recommend the ginger cake.

Finally, the shop, which is next to the reception. Many visitors like to buy a bag of our flour to take home. It's ground here, of course, and it's slightly more expensive than supermarket flour, but people say it makes wonderful bread. We also sell books about local history, but please note that the shop closes half an hour before the mill does, at four thirty.

Right, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start with the water wheel.

questions.why: 1300年代の記録は最初の水車小屋で、今の建物は1792年（18世紀後半）。

sets.script:
Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming to this information session for the Lakeside Ten K. I'm Fiona, and this is my fourth year organising the race. Whether you're a serious runner or you're planning to walk most of the way, I hope you'll find this useful.

Let me start with what's new this year. The biggest change is the start time. In previous years we started at ten, but it got very hot by the end of the race, so this year we're starting an hour earlier, at nine. The other new thing is that we've added a children's race, which is just two kilometres and starts at eight thirty, so parents can run with their children and still be ready for the main race. The entry fee, I'm afraid, hasn't changed, and the route is exactly the same as last year: one lap of the lake, then back along the river.

As always, the race is raising money for a local cause. Last year the money went to the hospital, and the year before that to the town library. This year, all the money raised will go to the town's youth sports clubs, which badly need new equipment.

Now, race numbers. A lot of people expect them to be sent by post, but because of the cost, we've stopped doing that. Instead, you collect your number from the sports centre on the Friday evening before the race, between five and eight. If you really can't make it on Friday, you can collect it on the morning of the race, but the queues can be very long, so please try to come on Friday.

On the course itself, there are two water stations, one at three kilometres and one at seven. There won't be any plastic bottles this year. Instead, we'll be handing out paper cups, which can be recycled. If you prefer, you can carry your own bottle and we'll fill it up for you.

There's a bag drop near the start, in the large white tent. It's free, but space is limited, so please bring only one small bag. Don't leave valuables like phones or wallets in your bag. The volunteers will look after the bags carefully, but we can't accept responsibility for anything inside them.

When you cross the finish line, please keep walking. It's very tempting to stop, but if people stand around at the finish, it quickly gets crowded and dangerous for the runners coming behind. Collect your medal from the volunteers, and then pick up your free banana and drink in the area just beyond. If you feel unwell at any point, the first aid team will be at the finish and at the halfway point.

A word about fund-raising. Every runner who raises more than a hundred pounds will receive a T-shirt, and the person who raises the most money will win a pair of running shoes donated by a local shop. Last year's winner raised over two thousand pounds, so the competition is serious.

And finally, the weather. People always ask me what happens if it rains. The answer is that the race goes ahead whatever the weather. The only thing that would stop us is very strong wind, because of the trees along the river path. If that happens, we'll put a message on the website by seven o'clock on the morning of the race.

Right, does anyone have any questions?

sets.script:
W: Hi, Tom. Have you got a few minutes to go through the library survey before we see Dr Marsh on Thursday?
M: Sure, Aisha. I've put all the results into a spreadsheet, so we can look at them together.
W: Great. I was thinking about how to start the presentation. Should we explain why we chose the topic?
M: I think so. People might assume we picked it because the data was easy to collect, but that's not really true. It took ages.
W: No, the main reason was that the university had just announced it was going to redesign the library, and we thought our results might actually be useful.
M: Exactly. And Dr Marsh only agreed to it after we'd already started, so we can't say it was her idea.
W: Right. Then we explain the method. We should mention that we planned an online questionnaire at first.
M: Yes, and that we dropped the idea because response rates for online surveys here are so low. Standing at the entrance with paper forms was much more effective, even if it was boring.
W: We got over four hundred forms back, which is good. So, the findings. What surprised you most?
M: Well, the computer result was exactly what I'd predicted. Hardly anyone uses the library computers, because almost everyone has a laptop now.
W: Same here, that was no surprise. What surprised me was how many students said they mainly study in groups. Nearly sixty per cent.
M: That's true. I'd assumed the library was mainly for silent study. And the other thing I hadn't expected was the timing. I thought evenings would be the busiest, but most people come between ten and two.
W: I'd guessed that, because of the timetable. But the group study figure was definitely a surprise for both of us.
M: And the time of day was a surprise for me, at least. Should we also talk about the problems with the survey?
W: We have to. The biggest one is that most of the forms were filled in by first-year students, so the results may not be typical of the whole university.
M: That's because we did it in the first term, when the first-years are around the library all the time. And the other problem was the question about the café.
W: Oh yes. Lots of people left it blank because they didn't understand whether we meant the café inside the library or the one next door.
M: So that's two problems: the sample and the unclear question. I don't think the length of the form was an issue, though. Most people finished it in under five minutes.
W: Agreed. Now, the last part is our opinions on the changes the university is proposing. Let's go through them. First, longer opening hours.
M: Honestly, I don't see the point. Our own data show that very few people are there late in the evening, so I don't think many students would benefit.
W: I'd have said it was important for students with jobs, but you're right, the numbers don't support it. OK, next: removing some of the bookshelves on the ground floor.
M: That one I'm more positive about. Some people will complain, but those shelves contain old journals that nobody uses, and they're all available online.
W: Yes, and the space could be used for something more useful. It's long overdue, really. What about the new café?
M: I like the idea, but I can't imagine where the money would come from. A kitchen, staff, furniture... it would cost a fortune.
W: That's what worries me too. And then the bookable group rooms.
M: Given our results, that seems the most obvious one to me. If sixty per cent of people study in groups, they need somewhere to talk without disturbing others.
W: Absolutely. I think we should make that our main recommendation.
M: Agreed. So what do we need to do before Thursday?
W: Well, I think the charts are fine, but we haven't written the conclusion yet.
M: Let's do that tomorrow afternoon. And maybe we should ask Dr Marsh whether she wants a written report as well as the presentation.
W: I'll email her tonight. Actually, I just remembered, she said in the first lecture that she only wants the slides and a one-page summary. So let's write the summary together tomorrow, after the conclusion.
M: Perfect.

sets.script:
W2: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your playground study?
W: Yes, thanks, Dr Okafor. We've finished the observations at the two primary schools, and we'd like some advice before we start writing up.
W2: Of course. Remind me what you were looking at.
M: We wanted to see whether the design of a playground affects how children play. One school, Hillside, has a traditional playground, just a large area of tarmac with some lines painted on it. The other, Brookfield, was redesigned two years ago with logs, sand, plants and some loose materials like crates and boxes.
W2: And how did you collect your data?
W: We spent ten lunchtimes at each school. We'd originally planned to film the children, but the schools weren't comfortable with that, which is understandable. So in the end we just observed and wrote notes every five minutes.
W2: That's a perfectly acceptable method. Did you have any problems?
M: The main one was that at Hillside it rained on four of the ten days, so the children stayed inside and we had to come back the following week.
W: And the other thing was that it was hard to watch everyone at once. Brookfield's playground has lots of corners and hidden spaces, so we probably missed some of the activity there.
W2: That's worth mentioning in your limitations section. So what did you find?
M: Well, the first thing was the amount of physical activity. We'd expected the children at Hillside to run around more, because there's so much open space. But in fact the levels were about the same at both schools.
W: The biggest difference was in the kind of play. At Hillside, most of the time was spent on organised games, mainly football, and they were dominated by a small group of older boys. At Brookfield, there was much more imaginative play. Children were building dens, making up stories, that kind of thing.
M: And at Brookfield, children of different ages played together much more. That was really noticeable.
W2: Interesting. What about conflict? People often worry that loose materials lead to arguments.
W: We thought so too, but there were fewer arguments at Brookfield, not more. The teachers there said the same thing.
W2: Good. Now, how are you planning to present the findings in your report?
M: We've got three ideas, and we can't agree. One is a table comparing the two schools; another is a set of photographs of the playgrounds; and the third is some quotes from the teachers we spoke to.
W2: What do you think of the table?
W: I think it's essential. It's the clearest way to show the numbers side by side.
M: I agree with that. The photos are where we disagree.
W: I think they'd really help a reader understand the difference between the two spaces.
M: But we'd need permission from the schools, and they'd have to be taken when no children are there. It's a lot of work for something that's not really data.
W2: I'd say Tom has a point. A simple plan of each playground would do the same job, and you can draw it yourselves.
W: OK, that's fair. A plan, then.
W2: And the teachers' quotes?
M: I'm not sure they're reliable. The teachers at Brookfield were obviously very proud of their playground.
W: But that's exactly why they're interesting. As long as we say clearly that they're opinions, they add something the observations can't.
W2: I agree with Sarah. Use a few, but don't rely on them.
M: Fine.
W2: One last thing. What are you going to recommend at the end?
W: We were going to say that all schools should redesign their playgrounds like Brookfield.
W2: I'd be careful. You only studied two schools, and they're different in other ways too. Brookfield is in a much smaller village, for example.
M: So should we just suggest that more research is needed?
W2: That's part of it. But I think your strongest point is about loose materials. They're very cheap, and any school could try them without a full redesign. I'd recommend that.
W: That's a good idea. Thank you, Dr Okafor.

sets.script:
M: OK, Jess, shall we go through the cinema case study? The assignment's due next Friday.
W: Yes, let's. I've read the reports on all three cinemas now. Did you manage to visit the Regent, Tom?

M: I did, on Saturday. It was much busier than I expected for a small independent cinema. And the manager was happy to talk to me for half an hour.
W: Brilliant. So the question we're answering is why some small cinemas survive when so many others have closed. What did the manager say was the main reason?
M: Well, I assumed she'd say it was the low ticket prices. They're about a third cheaper than the big chains. But she said that actually it's the programme. They show a mixture of new releases, older classics and foreign films, so people come back every week to see what's on.
W: That fits with what I found in the report on the Palace in Northgate. They tried cutting prices a few years ago, and it made almost no difference to audience numbers.
M: Interesting. What else did you find about the Palace?
W: Two things. They've started running film clubs for different groups, like one for parents with babies and one for older people in the afternoons. And they've opened a bar that stays open after the last film, so it's become a place where people meet.
M: The Regent has a café, but it closes at six, so that's not the same. Did the Palace do anything with schools?
W: The report mentions that they tried, but it didn't work because of transport costs. So that's not one of the reasons for their success.
M: OK. And the third one, the Majestic, closed last year, didn't it?
W: Yes. That's why I think it's useful, because it shows what can go wrong. The report says they spent a huge amount on new seats and a sound system, which is what the big chains do, but they couldn't compete with them on that.
M: So they were trying to be something they weren't.
W: Exactly. Now, for the assignment, we need to present our findings in some way. What do you think about using a chart to compare audience numbers?
M: I like the idea, but we only have figures for the Palace and the Majestic. The Regent manager wouldn't give me exact numbers.
W: Then a chart would be a bit misleading. Maybe a table showing the main features of each cinema instead?
M: That's better. We can include the things we know for all three.
W: And what about the interview? Should we include the whole thing?
M: No, it's far too long. I'll pick out the most useful parts.
W: Good. Now, the assignment also asks us to recommend something to a small cinema that's struggling. I was going to suggest cheaper tickets, but after what we've found, I don't think that's right.
M: No. I think the main recommendation should be the variety of films.
W: I agree that's important, but I'd put the social side first, like the bar and the clubs. People can watch films at home now. What they can't get at home is the feeling of being part of a community.
M: Hmm. I see what you mean, but I still think the programme is the reason people choose one cinema rather than another.
W: Why don't we present them as two equal recommendations? Then we can explain the argument for each one.
M: That's fair. What about the conclusion?
W: The lecturer said we should mention limitations. I think the obvious one is that we only looked at three cinemas, all in the same region.
M: And that most of our evidence comes from managers and reports written by the cinemas themselves. We didn't speak to any customers.
W: That's a really good point. Maybe we could do a short survey of customers at the Regent?
M: I'd love to, but we haven't got time before Friday. Let's just mention it as something future research could do.
W: OK. Shall we divide up the writing? You do the Regent and the interview, and I'll do the other two?
M: Fine. And we'll write the recommendations together.

questions.q: According to the Regent's manager, what is the main reason for its success?
choices: the range of films it shows
questions.why: 安い料金だと思ったが、マネージャーは it's the programme（いろいろな映画）と言った。

questions.q: What happened when the Palace reduced its ticket prices?
choices: The cinema lost a lot of money.
questions.why: it made almost no difference to audience numbers。

a bar that stays open late

questions.q: Why does Jess think the Majestic is useful for their study?
choices: It shows a strategy that failed.
It was the most successful of the three.

M2: Right, let's get started. You've both been working on the footpath erosion project in the national park. How's it going?
W: Pretty well, I think, Professor Hall. We've finished the fieldwork, and now we're looking at the data.
M2: Good. Just remind me what you measured.
M: We chose three paths that are used by different numbers of walkers, and at fixed points along each one we measured how wide the path was and how deep the ground had worn down.
M2: And how did you know how many walkers used each path?
W: The park authority has counters on the main paths, so we used their figures. We'd thought about counting walkers ourselves, but it would have taken weeks.
M2: Sensible. Were there any difficulties?
M: The weather was the biggest one. On two of our days it was so wet that the measurements weren't reliable, because the edges of the path were hard to see. We had to repeat them.
W: And we had trouble finding some of the fixed points again the second time. We'd marked them with small wooden posts, but a few had disappeared.
M2: That's common, I'm afraid. Probably sheep, or curious walkers. Next time, use GPS as well. So, what did you find?
W: Well, as you'd expect, the busiest path was the most eroded. But the relationship wasn't as simple as we thought.
M: Yes, the path with the middle number of walkers was actually wider than the busiest one in some places.
M2: Why do you think that was?
M: We think it's because of the surface. The busiest path has a stone surface on its steepest section, which was put in about ten years ago. The middle one doesn't have that, so when it's muddy, people walk on the grass at the side to avoid the mud, and the path gets wider and wider.
M2: That's a really important finding. What else?
W: The steepness made a big difference. On all three paths, the steepest sections were the most eroded, especially where water runs down the path after rain.
M2: Excellent. Now, the park authority is considering several ways to deal with erosion, and your report should comment on them. What do you think about putting in more stone surfaces?
W: I think the evidence supports it. Our results show it works, at least on steep sections.
M: I agree it works, but it's very expensive. Stone has to be carried up by helicopter in some places. I'd only recommend it for the worst sections.
M2: That's a fair point to include. What about closing paths for a period to let them recover?
W: I'm not keen. People would just make new paths round the closed ones, which would make things worse.
M: I'm less sure about that. If the closures were explained clearly, I think most walkers would accept them.
M2: Well, you can present both views. And what about signs asking people to stay on the path?
M: Our data suggest they don't work. There are signs on the middle path, and people still walk round the mud.
W: Yes, I'd say signs on their own are pretty useless. They'd need to be combined with something else, like better drainage.
M2: And drainage?
W: That's the one I'd most like to recommend. It's quite cheap, and it deals with the water, which seems to be the real cause of the damage.
M: I agree. If the water runs off the path, the mud doesn't form in the first place.
M2: Good. So, for the write-up, I'd suggest you include a map of the three paths, the results for each measuring point, and a section on the possible solutions. Do you have photographs?
W: Lots. But some of them aren't very clear because of the rain.
M2: Use only the best ones, and make sure each has a caption explaining what it shows. And the deadline is the end of the month, so you've got about three weeks.
M: Thanks, Professor Hall. That's really helpful.

sets.script:
Good morning. In today's lecture on the history of everyday objects, I'm going to talk about something most of us take completely for granted: the umbrella. It's a simple object, but its history tells us a great deal about social status, technology and, more recently, waste. I'll divide the lecture into four sections: the origins of the umbrella, its arrival in Europe, the changes in how it was made, and finally the environmental problems it causes today. Please keep your questions until the end, as we have a lot to get through.

Let's begin with its origins. When we think of umbrellas, we naturally think of rain. But the earliest umbrellas, which appear in carvings and paintings from several ancient civilisations, were not designed for rain at all. They were used for protection from the sun. In fact, the word umbrella comes from the Latin word for shade.

In these early societies, umbrellas were not something ordinary people carried. They were held over kings, priests and other important figures by servants, and they were a clear sign of status. In some courts, the number of umbrellas carried in front of a ruler showed how powerful he was.

The first umbrellas that could keep out rain were probably developed in China. They were made from paper stretched over a bamboo frame, and the paper was covered with wax, which made it waterproof. Later, oil was also used for the same purpose, but wax seems to have come first.

Over the following centuries, the idea spread along trade routes, and travellers' accounts describe umbrellas of many different shapes and sizes, some so large that they needed two people to carry them. In most places, though, they remained objects of ceremony rather than practical tools.

Now let's move to Europe. Umbrellas were known in Europe for centuries, but for a long time they were considered suitable only for women. When men in eighteenth-century Britain started carrying them in the rain, they were often laughed at in the street. And there was another group who disliked umbrellas: the drivers of horse-drawn coaches, who earned money by taking people home when it rained. They saw the umbrella as a direct threat to their business, and there are reports of drivers deliberately splashing umbrella users with mud.

Gradually, however, the umbrella became respectable, and by the nineteenth century it had become an essential accessory for a gentleman. This brings us to technology. Early European umbrellas were heavy and awkward, because their frames were made of wood or whalebone. Whalebone was flexible, but it was expensive and tended to break. The big change came in the eighteen-fifties, when steel frames replaced whalebone. Steel was lighter and much stronger, and the basic design hasn't changed very much since then.

For wealthy customers, umbrellas were also an opportunity to show off. The cover was usually made of silk, but it was the handle that attracted the most attention. Handles were carved from ivory or made of silver, and some even contained small compartments for keeping things like matches.

In the twentieth century, the most important development was the folding umbrella. Earlier umbrellas were long and had to be carried like a walking stick. Folding umbrellas could be made small enough to fit in a handbag, and this is the main reason they became so popular, especially in cities, where people travel on public transport.

Finally, let's consider the umbrella today, because there is a problem. Modern umbrellas are cheap, but they are also very difficult to recycle. They combine metal, plastic and fabric, and separating these materials costs more than the materials are worth. As a result, almost all broken umbrellas end up in landfill.

And umbrellas break very easily. You'll all have seen the bins in city centres full of broken umbrellas after storms. Some estimates suggest that more than a billion umbrellas are thrown away worldwide every year.

So what can be done? Some designers are working on umbrellas that can be taken apart, so that each material can be recycled separately. Others are returning to traditional materials. One company, for example, is producing umbrellas with frames made from bamboo, which is strong, light and grows very quickly. And a number of cities have introduced umbrella-sharing schemes, where people can borrow an umbrella at a station and return it at another.

In the next lecture, we'll look at another everyday object with a surprisingly long history: the pencil.

Good afternoon, everyone. Today we're continuing our series on urban environments by looking at a phenomenon called the urban heat island. This is the simple observation that cities are often noticeably warmer than the countryside around them. On a calm summer day, the difference might be one or two degrees. But the difference is usually greatest at night, when the countryside cools down quickly and the city doesn't. In some large cities, temperatures at night can be as much as seven or eight degrees higher than in nearby rural areas.

Before we look at the causes, a word about how the effect is measured. Traditionally, scientists compared readings from weather stations in the city centre with readings from stations in the countryside. The problem is that there are relatively few stations, so the picture was incomplete. Today, satellites can measure the temperature of surfaces across an entire city, and this has shown that the heat is not spread evenly. Some neighbourhoods, often the poorer ones with fewer parks, are much hotter than others.

So why does this happen? There are several causes, and I'll go through the main ones.

The first is the materials that cities are built from. Natural surfaces like grass and soil reflect some of the sun's energy and also contain water, which cools the ground as it evaporates. In a city, by contrast, much of the ground is covered by dark surfaces such as roads and roofs. These absorb heat during the day and then release it slowly during the night, which is why cities stay warm after sunset.

The second cause is heat produced directly by human activity. You might think that factories would be the main source, but in most modern cities that isn't the case. The biggest contributors are traffic and air conditioning units, which pump warm air out into the street. There's an obvious irony here: the hotter the city becomes, the more people use air conditioning, and the hotter the city becomes.

The third cause is the shape of the city itself. Tall buildings close together create what are sometimes called urban canyons. These trap heat, and they also reduce the wind, which would otherwise carry warm air away.

Why does all this matter? Firstly, there are clear effects on health. During heatwaves, cities see a sharp rise in illness, and the people most at risk are elderly people, especially those who live alone, because nobody notices when they start to become unwell. Young children are also vulnerable, but studies suggest that isolation is the most important single factor.

Secondly, there are economic costs. Higher temperatures increase the demand for electricity, mainly for cooling, and this can put pressure on supply during the hottest weeks. Thirdly, heat affects the quality of the air, because some pollutants form more quickly at higher temperatures.

So what can cities do? The good news is that many of the solutions are relatively simple. One is to change the colour of surfaces. Painting roofs white, for example, means that they reflect sunlight instead of absorbing it. Some cities now require all new flat roofs to be painted in a light colour.

A second approach, and probably the most effective, is planting trees. Trees provide shade, which keeps both people and buildings cool, and they also release water vapour through their leaves. Research in several cities has found that streets with a lot of trees can be several degrees cooler than streets with none.

Green roofs, which are roofs covered with plants, are another option. They're more expensive than simply painting a roof, but they have an additional benefit, which is that they reduce flooding, because they hold rainwater instead of letting it run straight into the drains.

Finally, there's the question of urban planning. When new districts are designed, the position and height of buildings can be arranged to let air move through the streets. In coastal cities, for example, planners are designing new streets so that cool breezes from the sea can pass through them, rather than being blocked by a wall of tall buildings.

None of these measures is a complete answer on its own, but together they can make a real difference. In our next session, we'll look at a case study of one city that has tried to combine all of them.

Good morning. In this lecture I want to look at glass in the Roman world. Glass is so ordinary today that it's easy to forget it was once a luxury, and the Roman period is when that began to change.

Glass had been made for well over a thousand years before the Romans. But early glass objects were produced by slow and difficult methods. The most common was to pour hot glass into moulds, or to build up layers of glass around a core of clay. These methods produced beautiful objects, but they took a long time, and only the rich could afford them.

The key change was the invention of glassblowing, which happened some time in the first century BC, probably somewhere on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean. By blowing air through a long tube into a ball of hot glass, a skilled worker could make a bottle or a cup in a matter of minutes. The effect was dramatic. Glass became cheap, and within a few generations it was being used in ordinary homes across the empire.

What did people use it for? Above all, for storing and serving food and drink. Pottery had been used for this for centuries, but glass had an important advantage: it did not affect the taste of the food. Wine, oil, honey and medicines were all kept in glass. And because glass is transparent, people could see what was inside a container without opening it.

Glass was also used for decoration. Small cubes of coloured glass were used in mosaics on walls and ceilings, where they caught the light in a way that stone could not. Glass beads were worn as jewellery and traded far beyond the borders of the empire, and they have been found by archaeologists as far away as northern Europe and central Asia.

That brings me to the question of colour. Most Roman glass was not perfectly clear. Natural glass usually had a slightly green colour, which came from small amounts of iron in the sand used to make it. For everyday bottles, this didn't matter. But for high-quality tableware, glassmakers wanted colourless glass, and they discovered that adding a mineral called manganese removed the green tint. This was a skilled process, and colourless glass was always more expensive.

The Romans were also the first to use glass in windows on any scale. Window glass was first used in public baths, where it allowed light in while keeping the heat inside. Later it spread to the villas of the wealthy. However, we shouldn't imagine Roman windows as being like ours. The glass was thick and uneven, and you couldn't really see through it. Its purpose was to let in light, not to give a view.

One thing that surprises students is how much the Romans recycled glass. Broken glass was valuable because it melts at a lower temperature than the raw materials, which saves fuel. There's good evidence that broken glass was collected in towns and sold back to glassmakers. The most striking example is a shipwreck found off the coast of southern France, which was carrying several tonnes of broken glass, almost certainly on its way to be recycled.

What about the people who made it? Glass workshops were usually small, family businesses. In many towns they were located outside the town walls. You might think this was because of the smoke, which must have been unpleasant, but the main reason was the risk of fire. Furnaces burned day and night, and in towns full of wooden buildings, a single accident could be a disaster.

Finally, a word about current research. One of the big questions archaeologists ask is where a piece of glass was made. Today they can answer this by analysing its chemistry. Because the sand used in different regions has a slightly different chemical make-up, a tiny sample can reveal which area the sand came from. This has shown that raw glass was often produced in just a few large centres and then shipped all over the empire to be shaped by local workshops.

Next week we'll move on to metalwork.

Hello, everyone. In today's marketing lecture we're going to look at the role of colour in product packaging. When you walk into a shop, you're surrounded by thousands of products, and research suggests that shoppers often decide which one to pick up in just a few seconds. In that short time, colour does a lot of the work. We notice colour before we notice shapes, and long before we read any words on a package.

It's worth remembering that this is a fairly recent situation. Until the early twentieth century, most goods were sold loose, and the shopkeeper weighed out what the customer wanted. Packaging became important only when self-service shops appeared, because suddenly the package itself had to persuade the customer, with no shop assistant to help. From that moment, manufacturers began to think very carefully about how their products looked on the shelf.

Let's start with some of the associations that colours commonly have,
 at least in Europe and North America. Red is linked with energy and excitement. It also attracts attention very quickly, which is why it's often used for special offers. You'll see a lot of red on sports drinks, for example, where the message is about power and activity.

Blue, on the other hand, tends to suggest calm and trust. That's why it's so popular with banks and insurance companies, but on food packaging it's less common, partly because there are very few naturally blue foods.

Green used to mean simply that something was natural. Nowadays, however, so many products use green that the association has become rather weak, and some consumers have become suspicious of it.

What about black? For many years, black packaging was avoided because it was considered too serious, even depressing. But today it's strongly associated with luxury. Think of expensive chocolates or cosmetics. And white is used to suggest simplicity, which is why it's popular with technology companies that want their products to seem easy to use.

I should stress, though, that these associations are not universal. Purple is a good example. In many European countries, it has been associated with royalty for centuries, because purple dye was once extremely expensive. In other parts of the world, it carries quite different meanings, so international brands have to be careful.

How do researchers study the effect of colour? Asking people directly isn't very useful, because shoppers are often unaware of why they choose one product over another. So one common method is eye tracking. A small camera records exactly where a person looks on a shelf and for how long. This shows which packages are noticed first.

Some of the most interesting research has looked at whether colour affects how products actually taste. In one well-known type of experiment, people are given exactly the same crisps in packets of different colours. Many participants report that the crisps in the blue packet taste less salty than the ones in the red packet, even though they're identical. In other words, the colour of the package changes our expectations, and our expectations change our experience.

So colour is powerful. But there's a problem. When one brand succeeds with a particular colour, its competitors often copy it. Eventually, if too many brands in a category use the same colour, all the products start to look similar, and colour stops helping any of them stand out. Marketers sometimes call this the sea of sameness.

So what's the future? There are two trends I want to mention. The first is that more and more shopping is done online, where products appear as small images on a screen. In online shopping, colour may matter less than it does in a physical shop, because shoppers usually search for a product by name.

The second trend is that some brands are now trying to stand out through texture rather than colour. Packages with an unusual feel, such as a rough or soft surface, encourage customers to pick them up, and research suggests that once a product is in someone's hand, they're much more likely to buy it.

For next week, I'd like you to choose one product category and photograph the shelf in a local shop. We'll analyse the colours together.

sets.passage:
The return of the beaver

For four hundred years there were no beavers in Britain. The animals had been hunted to extinction by the sixteenth century, mainly for their fur and for a substance called castoreum, which was used in medicine and perfume. Then, in 2009, a small number of beavers from Norway were released in a remote part of western Scotland. It was the first time a mammal had been officially reintroduced to the United Kingdom, and the project was watched closely by scientists, farmers and conservationists alike.

Britain was far from the only country to have lost its beavers. By the end of the nineteenth century, only around a thousand of the animals survived in the whole of Europe, scattered in a handful of isolated river valleys. Legal protection and a long series of reintroductions in more than twenty countries have since transformed the picture, and the European population is now thought to exceed a million.

The Eurasian beaver is the largest rodent in Europe. An adult can weigh more than twenty kilograms, and its broad, flat tail, which is covered in scales, is used both for steering in the water and as a warning signal: when danger approaches, a beaver slaps its tail loudly on the surface. Beavers live in family groups, usually a pair of adults and their young from the previous two years, and they share a home called a lodge, a large pile of sticks and mud whose entrance lies under water, out of reach of predators. Contrary to popular belief, beavers do not eat fish. Their diet consists entirely of plants: leaves, grasses and, in winter, the bark of trees.

The Scottish release was designed as a trial. Over five years, researchers monitored the health of the animals, their effect on the surrounding woodland and the attitudes of local people. Meanwhile, a second, unplanned population had appeared on the River Tay, further east, where beavers had either escaped from private collections or been released illegally. By the time the official trial ended, the Tay beavers far outnumbered those in the trial area, which made the debate about whether beavers should be allowed to stay in Scotland somewhat academic.

Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers. Using their strong front teeth, they fell young trees and drag the branches into streams to build dams. Behind each dam, a pond forms. These ponds slow the flow of water, trap sediment and create wetlands that support frogs, dragonflies, fish and birds. A study in Devon, in the south-west of England, found that a single family of beavers had built thirteen dams along one stream over six years, and that the number of plant species on the site had almost doubled.

The animals also appear to help with two problems that worry many British communities: flooding and drought. During heavy rain, water is held back in the ponds and released slowly, so villages downstream are less likely to flood. In dry summers, the same ponds keep the land around them moist. Researchers measured the water leaving the Devon site after a storm and found that the peak flow was roughly a third lower than at a similar stream without beavers.

Not everyone welcomes the beavers' return, however. Some farmers have complained that dams flood productive fields and that fallen trees block drainage channels. Anglers have raised concerns that dams may stop salmon and trout from swimming upstream to breed, although the evidence on this question is mixed. In response, the Scottish government introduced a licensing system in 2019 that allows landowners to move or, in some cases, remove beavers that cause serious damage.

Supporters argue that most conflicts can be managed with simple tools. A pipe placed through a dam, for example, lets excess water escape and keeps the pond at a safe level. Wire mesh around the base of a valuable tree stops the animals from cutting it down. In Devon, a local group pays for such measures from a fund supported by tourism, since visitors now travel to the area specifically in the hope of seeing a beaver at dusk.

By 2023, wild beavers were living in at least fifteen river systems across Britain, and the government in England had begun to accept applications for further releases. The animals' comeback is still small in scale, but it has changed the way many people think about the countryside. Instead of asking only how land can be protected from water, planners are beginning to ask how water, and the creatures that shape it, might protect the land.

sets.passage:
The humble pencil

Few objects are as familiar as the pencil, and few are taken so completely for granted. Yet the pencil has a long and surprising history, and the story of how it reached its modern form involves shepherds, smugglers, chemists and an entire industry built in the forests of central Europe.

The story begins in the hills of northern England in the sixteenth century. According to local accounts, a violent storm uprooted a tree and exposed a deposit of a soft, black, shiny material beneath it. Local shepherds soon discovered that it left a dark mark on whatever it touched, and they began using it to mark their sheep so that each owner could recognise his animals. The material was graphite, a form of carbon, but at the time nobody understood what it was. Because it looked rather like lead, people called it black lead, and the name has stayed with us: even today, we talk about the lead in a pencil, although pencils have never contained any lead at all.

The deposit turned out to be unusually pure, and it was solid enough to be cut into sticks. No other source of such high-quality graphite was known anywhere in the world, and it quickly became extremely valuable. Apart from its use for writing, it was used to line the moulds in which cannonballs were made, which gave it military importance. The mine was guarded, and at one point it was deliberately flooded between periods of extraction to stop people from stealing the graphite. Even so, smuggling was common, and in the eighteenth century a law was passed that made stealing graphite a serious crime.

The earliest pencils were simply sticks of graphite, and they had obvious disadvantages: they were brittle, and they left the user's fingers black. At first people wrapped them in string or sheepskin to hold them. Later, craftsmen began to place the graphite inside a holder made of wood. A groove was cut in one strip of wood, the graphite was inserted, and a second strip was glued on top. This basic method is still used today, although the process is now carried out by machines rather than by hand.

The next major development came from France at the end of the eighteenth century. France was at war with Britain and could no longer obtain English graphite. A French engineer was asked to find an alternative, and his solution was to grind poor-quality graphite into a powder, mix it with clay and water, and then heat the mixture in a kiln. The result was a pencil core that was both strong and smooth. Crucially, the method also made it possible to control how hard or soft a pencil was: more clay produced a harder pencil that made a lighter line, while more graphite produced a softer pencil with a darker line. The system of grading pencils that artists and engineers still use developed from this discovery.

During the nineteenth century, pencil manufacture became a large industry, centred on the region around Nuremberg in Germany, where several family firms competed fiercely. The best pencils were made with cedar wood, which is soft enough to sharpen easily but does not split. As forests of suitable cedar became harder to find, manufacturers began to look further afield for supplies, and today much of the wood used comes from managed plantations.

Many people have wondered why so many pencils are painted yellow. One popular explanation is that in the late nineteenth century, a manufacturer began selling pencils made with high-quality graphite from East Asia and painted them yellow, a colour associated with luxury in that region, to suggest their quality. Whether or not this story is entirely true, yellow became the standard colour for pencils in North America, while in parts of Europe red or green pencils are just as common.

The eraser on the end of the pencil is a later addition. The first patent for a pencil with an attached eraser was granted in the United States in the middle of the nineteenth century. Interestingly, the idea did not catch on everywhere: many European pencils are still sold without erasers, partly because some teachers believe that students should not be encouraged to correct their mistakes too easily.

Despite the arrival of computers and tablets, the pencil has not disappeared. Billions are still produced every year. It is cheap, it works in any temperature, it does not need electricity, and its marks can be removed. For a tool that began as a way of marking sheep, it has proved remarkably difficult to replace.

sets.passage:
The longest journey

Every year, a small grey and white seabird completes what is thought to be the longest migration of any animal on Earth. The Arctic tern breeds in the far north, in places such as Greenland, Iceland and northern Canada, during the brief Arctic summer. When the breeding season ends, it flies south, past the coasts of Europe and Africa or South America, all the way to the edge of Antarctica, where it spends the southern summer. Then it returns north again to breed.

For a long time, scientists could only estimate the length of this journey. Birds were fitted with small metal rings on their legs, and occasionally a ringed bird would be found thousands of kilometres from where it had been ringed. These records proved that terns travelled between the two polar regions, but they revealed little about the routes the birds took or how long the journey lasted.

The picture changed when researchers began to use tiny tracking devices called geolocators. These devices, which weigh less than two grams, record the amount of daylight at regular intervals. From the times of sunrise and sunset, scientists can calculate the approximate position of the bird each day. In one study, geolocators were attached to a group of terns breeding in Greenland and Iceland. Because the devices store their data rather than transmitting it, they can only be read once they have been removed from the bird. When the birds returned a year later and the devices were recovered, the results were astonishing. The average distance travelled during the year was around 70,000 kilometres, and some individuals covered considerably more.

The study also showed that the terns do not fly directly from north to south. Instead, they follow a route shaped roughly like the letter S across the Atlantic. This appears to allow them to take advantage of the prevailing winds, which means they use less energy than they would if they flew in a straight line. The tracking data also revealed that, on the southward journey, most of the birds stopped for several weeks in an area of the North Atlantic, far from land, where cold water rises from the deep sea and brings with it large amounts of food. Here the birds were able to build up the reserves of fat they would need for the rest of the journey. On the return flight in spring, by contrast, the terns travelled much faster and made fewer stops, possibly because arriving early at the breeding grounds gives a bird a better chance of securing a good nesting site. The northward journey took, on average, about forty days, compared with around ninety days for the journey south.

The Arctic tern is not a large bird. An adult weighs only about a hundred grams, less than a typical mobile phone. It is, however, extremely long-lived for a bird of its size, and individuals are known to have survived for more than thirty years. Over such a lifetime, a tern may fly a total distance equivalent to travelling to the Moon and back three times.

Because it spends the summer in the Arctic and then a second summer in the Antarctic, the Arctic tern experiences more daylight than any other animal. This is useful, because the tern feeds by sight. It hovers above the water, looking for small fish and shrimp-like animals near the surface, and then dives to catch them. Long hours of daylight mean long hours of feeding.

Arctic terns nest in colonies, often on small islands or along stony beaches, where they lay their eggs directly on the ground with little or no nest material. The eggs are well camouflaged, which protects them from some predators, but the adults also defend their nests aggressively. Anyone who walks too close to a colony is likely to be attacked from the air, and the birds frequently strike intruders on the head with their sharp beaks. Experienced visitors to tern colonies often wear a hat or carry a stick above their heads, because the birds tend to aim at the highest point.

Although the Arctic tern is not currently considered to be in danger, scientists are watching it closely. Because it depends on the conditions at both ends of the Earth and at several points in between, it may be particularly sensitive to changes in the environment. In some breeding colonies, a shortage of the small fish that terns feed their chicks has led to years in which very few young birds survived. Researchers hope that the tracking studies, which are now being carried out at colonies in several countries, will help to identify the places along the route that matter most to the birds, so that these areas can be protected.

sets.passage:
Ice before refrigerators

Today, ice is something most people can make in their own kitchens without thinking about it. But for most of human history, ice in warm weather was a rare luxury, and keeping it from melting required considerable effort and ingenuity.

The earliest known methods of storing ice come from dry, hot regions. In parts of ancient Persia, people built large domed structures above deep pits. In winter, water was channelled into shallow pools beside the structure, where it froze during the cold desert nights. The ice was then cut and placed in the pit, which was insulated by thick walls made of a special mixture of clay, sand and other materials. Ice stored in this way could last through the hot summer months and was used to cool drinks and to make chilled desserts. Some of these structures were large enough to hold thousands of cubic metres of ice, and a few of them can still be seen today.

The idea of keeping winter ice for summer use was not limited to Persia. Records from ancient China describe ice being collected from rivers and stored in cellars, and in parts of the Mediterranean, snow was carried down from the mountains and kept in pits covered with branches and leaves. In each case, the basic principle was the same: ice melts more slowly when it is kept in large quantities, away from sunlight and protected from warm air.


In Europe, the use of ice houses became widespread among wealthy landowners in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. A typical ice house was a brick chamber, often shaped like an egg, built partly or wholly underground. It was usually placed on a north-facing slope or among trees, where it would receive as little sun as possible. In winter, workers cut blocks of ice from frozen lakes and ponds on the estate and carried them to the ice house, where they were packed tightly together. Layers of straw were placed between and around the blocks to provide insulation. A drain at the bottom carried away the water from any ice that did melt, since standing water would cause the rest of the ice to melt more quickly.

A well-built ice house could keep ice for a year or even longer. The ice was used in the kitchen to preserve food such as fish and meat, to make ice cream, which was a fashionable dessert among the rich, and sometimes for medical purposes, for instance to reduce a patient's fever. For the people who owned them, ice houses were also a symbol of wealth, since only a large estate could afford the labour needed to fill one.

In the nineteenth century, ice became a commercial product on a huge scale. Merchants in the north-east of the United States discovered that ice cut from frozen lakes in winter could be shipped to hot countries, packed in sawdust, and still arrive in usable condition. At first, many people thought the idea was ridiculous, and early shipments lost money. But the trade grew rapidly, and ice was eventually exported to the Caribbean, South America and even India, a voyage that took several months.

Britain, too, imported large quantities of natural ice, much of it from Norway, where the cold climate and the many lakes close to the coast made it easy to harvest and transport. The ice arrived by ship and was stored in enormous ice wells, some of them more than ten metres deep, before being delivered to fishmongers, restaurants and private homes. In cities, ice was sold from carts, and households that could afford it kept a wooden cabinet lined with metal, known as an icebox, in which a block of ice kept food cool for a day or two.

The natural ice trade had its problems, however. A mild winter could mean that there was not enough ice to harvest, and prices rose sharply. There were also growing concerns about cleanliness, because ice taken from lakes and rivers might contain dirt or be contaminated by waste. These concerns encouraged the development of machines that could produce ice artificially from clean water. The first such machines appeared in the middle of the nineteenth century, and by the early twentieth century, factory-made ice had largely replaced natural ice in most industrialised countries.

The final step was the arrival of the electric refrigerator in ordinary homes, which happened gradually during the twentieth century. With it, the need for ice houses, ice ships and ice carts disappeared. Many of the old ice houses still survive on country estates, but most are now empty. Some have found an unexpected new role: their cool, dark and stable conditions make them ideal places for bats to spend the winter, and conservation groups have adapted several of them for this purpose.
